R2:physical.title: Turbulent flow by direct numerical simulation
R2:physical.summary: Compute-bound. The Navier-Stokes equations are solved with no turbulence model, and cost grows as Re^3. Most industrial flows are beyond the largest computers (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_numerical_simulation). My arithmetic: 1000x more compute buys only about 10x in Reynolds number. The cheap workarounds (RANS, LES) give up accuracy to save compute.

R2:physical.title: Training robot foundation models and video world models
R2:physical.summary: Compute-heavy and partly compute-bound. Cosmos used 10,000 H100s for three months on about 20M hours of video (arxiv.org/html/2501.03575v1). By my arithmetic that is about 21.6M GPU-hours. GEN-0 needs about 7B parameters to absorb its data (generalistai.com/blog/gen-0, via framer). These models inherit their data's gaps, including missing touch (rodneybrooks.com, via framer).

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?

plan.option_title: Turbulent flow by direct numerical simulation
plan.question: Does a validated GPU spectral turbulence simulation on one rented 8-GPU node show cost per large-eddy turnover rising with Reynolds number, as the claimed Re³ law predicts?
plan.hypothesis: Cost per large-eddy turnover will scale roughly as N⁴, i.e. Rλ⁶, so 100× compute buys only about 2.15× in Rλ [wiki_dns].

compute_axis.quantity: grid points per side N at fixed small-scale resolution (k_max η ≈ 1.35), which sets Rλ and cost

held_fixed: same pseudo-spectral scheme (integrating factor, AB2, phase-shift de-aliasing, forcing |k|≤2)
same JHTDB starting field low-pass filtered

predictions.if_lever: Fitted exponents near a≈2/3 (Rλ∝N^a), b≈4 (dollars per T_L∝N^b), c≈6 (∝Rλ^c): extra compute buys little Reynolds number.
predictions.if_not: Fitted exponents differ clearly from 2/3, 4 and 6 with confidence intervals excluding them, e.g. because u′ and ε do not stay fixed across rungs.
predictions.decision_rule: Compare fitted a, b, c with 2/3, 4, 6 using confidence intervals; the Re³ scaling is supported if the intervals contain the predictions.
predictions.noise_rule: Report confidence intervals on the exponent fits; JHTDB's own scatter (Rλ std 10.8, window means 406.6–432.9) sets the statistical tolerances; fits made with and without the latency-dominated 128³ rung.
predictions.expected_why: The file's own derivation from JHTDB definitions gives N⁴ ∝ Rλ⁶ and the plan expects a≈2/3, b≈4, c≈6.

plan.compute_tested_why: The resolution ladder 128³ to 1024³ varies N, which is what more parallel GPU compute buys, and measures dollars and Rλ at each rung.
plan.scored_against: JHTDB isotropic1024 published time-averaged statistics (Rλ 418, ε 0.103, E 0.705, spectrum), stored frames, and the predicted exponents a≈2/3, b≈4, c≈6.

checks: C1: Taylor–Green exact solution relative L2 error ≤1e-10 at t=1; max relative divergence ≤1e-12; inviscid AB2 order between 1.8 and 2.2; forced-band energy constant to 1e-12; budget residual ≤1%; 1 vs 8 GPU agreement ≤1e-12 after 100 steps

C4: report u′, L, T_L, ε/(u′³/L) on every rung to test the fixed u′ and ε assumption

restructuring.sequential_part: Time stepping: about 50,280 sequential steps at 1024³, each depending on the previous one.
restructuring.method: Each 3D FFT is split across 8 GPUs in slabs, with an NCCL all-to-all transpose, so the transforms within one time step run in parallel.

novelty.closest_prior: JHTDB isotropic1024 is a published 1024³ pseudo-spectral DNS at Rλ 418 with stored fields; Wikipedia states DNS operations grow as Re³. Neither gives measured dollars per turnover on rented GPUs.
novelty.left_open: A measured dollars-versus-Rλ curve on rented hardware, with fitted exponents and an open validated solver, is not given by the cited sources.

limits: Cost per step is only bandwidth arithmetic until the bake-off measures it. Only one node and one forcing scheme; JHTDB scheme details may leave a mismatch floor. JHTDB cutout access was unconfirmed (HTTP 503).

pick.title: Training robot foundation models and video world models

plan.option_title: W13 made concrete: a $1,000 compute-versus-data experiment on a small robot foundation model
plan.question: With data held fixed, does more fine-tuning compute raise task success of a small robot vision-language-action model in simulation, or does data limit it?
plan.hypothesis: At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps shifts success under 3 points; more data adds 10 or more points [arXiv 2506.01844].

compute_axis.quantity: training steps per run (with fixed cosine schedule per run), crossed with data fraction; also trainable parameters in arm C

held_fixed: Model SmolVLA 0.45B with LeRobot defaults (lr 1e-4, AdamW betas 0.9/0.95, 1000 warmup, cosine to 2.5e-6, chunk 50)
Dataset lerobot/libero with pinned revision and pinned LeRobot commit
Nested task-stratified data subsets from one fixed shuffle seed
Evaluation: 50 episodes per task x 40 tasks, same seed, init_states true, n_action_steps chosen once before scoring the grid
Per-run cosine schedule with scheduler_decay_steps equal to steps in arm B

predictions.if_lever: At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps (3.3x compute) raises average success by 3 points or more, so compute still buys success.
predictions.if_not: At each data level, 15k to 50k steps moves success under 3 points; at 50k steps, 100% data beats 25% by 10 or more points.
predictions.decision_rule: P1: if the 15k to 50k change in average success is under 3 points at every data level, data-bound (not compute-bound); if 3 points or more, compute still pays. P2: 100% vs 25% data at 50k steps gap of at least 10 points means data is binding.
predictions.noise_rule: Count an effect as real only if it exceeds both the paired evaluation interval (about +/-2.1 points between two 2,000-episode cells; McNemar and task bootstrap) and twice the training-seed standard deviation from the B' replicates plus arm A.
predictions.expected_why: The paper says the model can be trained for far fewer steps without significant loss, and data scarcity (about 11 demos per task at 25%) should bind.

plan.compute_tested_why: Training steps vary 10x (5k to 50k) and trainable parameters about 4.5x, independently of data fraction, though far below the 100-1000x frontier range.
plan.scored_against: Simulated LIBERO success flag over 2,000 rollouts per checkpoint (50 per task x 40 tasks), compared within the grid against the B (100% data, 50k steps) cell and its B' replicate, and the harness against the published pi0.5 score.

arms.what: Evaluation-only harness check: score lerobot/pi05_libero_finetuned with n_action_steps=10
Replication gate: 2 seeds (1000, 1001), LeRobot LIBERO command unchanged, 100% data, default schedule, 100k steps
Compute x data grid: 12 runs, data in {10,25,50,100}% x steps in {5k,15k,50k}, decay steps = steps
4 seed replicates (seed 1001) of B's four 50k-step cells
Trainable capacity: train_expert_only=false freeze_vision_encoder=false, data 25% and 100%, 50k steps
Missing-channel analogue: wrist camera image2 removed, 100% data, 5k/15k/50k steps
Start from lerobot/smolvla_base (pretrained on another robot), data 25% and 100%, 50k steps

baseline.what: SmolVLA 0.45B published LIBERO average success (90/96/92/71 on Spatial/Object/Goal/Long), 100k steps at batch 64, no robot pretraining

anchor.what: Harness gate: LeRobot's published pi0.5 LIBERO checkpoint scored by our evaluator on 400 episodes must reach at least 94%; published value 97.5%.
anchor.tolerance: pass at 94% or above (binomial 95% band +/-1.5 points at 400 episodes); arm A replication mean within +/-5 points of 87.3

checks: Harness gate: pi0.5 checkpoint >= 94% on 400 episodes before any training
Replication gate: arm A mean within +/-5 of 87.3; early soft gate: 20k checkpoint at about hour 6 below 70% pauses the grid

records.card: **W13 · Training robot foundation models and video world models.** R2 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · halted: cost record broken **Question.** With data held fixed, does more fine-tuning compute raise task success of a small robot vision-language-action model in simulation, or does data limit it? **What is known.** SmolVLA paper reports LIBERO results at 0.24B/0.45B/2.25B sizes and says it can train for far fewer steps without significant loss, but gives no step or data grid [smolvla_paper]. Whether, at fixed data, more fine-tuning steps help SmolVLA on LIBERO, and how steps trade against data fraction, capacity and a removed camera. **Hypothesis.** At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps shifts success under 3 points; more data adds 10 or more points [arXiv 2506.01844]. **If compute is the lever.** At fixed data, 15k to 50k steps (3.3x compute) raises average success by 3 points or more, so compute still buys success. **If not.** At each data level, 15k to 50k steps moves success under 3 points; at 50k steps, 100% data beats 25% by 10 or more points. **Test.** Fine-tune SmolVLA on LIBERO in 25 runs, varying steps (5k, 15k, 50k) and data (10 to 100%) independently, plus capacity, camera removal and pretraining arms. Score 27 checkpoints on 2,000 rollouts each against a published 87.3% baseline. *Compute axis.* Training steps per run (with fixed cosine schedule per run), crossed with data fraction; also trainable parameters in arm C: 5,000–50,000 steps, 3 levels. Closest prior: 100,000 [smolvla_paper], not beyond it. Prior art checked without web search. *Restructuring.* none. **Check first.** Harness gate: LeRobot's published pi0.5 LIBERO checkpoint scored by our evaluator on 400 episodes must reach at least 94%; published value 97.5%. Tolerance: pass at 94% or above (binomial 95% band +/-1.5 points at 400 episodes); arm A replication mean within +/-5 points of 87.3. **Would not show.** Small simulated benchmark, one model family; may not transfer to larger models or real robots. Training and evaluation speed unmeasured, so cost may rise. 87.3% replication may miss; schedule unpublished. *Cost.* Plans $557.20 of the $1,000 budget over 35 machine-hours, leaving $442.80.
